passages.t: Grace and peace, and thanks for faith, love and hope
passages.happening:
The letter opens with its senders and its readers: “Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace and peace to you” (verse 1).

Then Paul gives thanks. “We always thank God for all of you, remembering you in our prayers and continually recalling before our God and Father your work of faith, your labor of love, and your enduring hope in our Lord Jesus Christ” (verses 2-3).
passages.hearers:
This is very likely the oldest of Paul's letters that we have. A few months before, these people had been worshipping the gods of a Greek city. Now they hear themselves called ‘the church’, and they hear where that church lives. Not only in Thessalonica, but ‘in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ’. Their address is a city on a map. Their home is in God.

Notice that Jesus is named right beside the Father, in the same breath, as the one in whom the church lives. Twenty years after the cross, in a letter to new believers from a pagan world, this is how the first Christians already spoke of him.

‘Grace and peace’ joins a Greek greeting and a Jewish one. Grace is God's free kindness. Peace is the old Hebrew wish for wholeness and well-being. Both come from God, and Paul puts both at the top of almost every letter he wrote.

Then comes a three-part thanks: faith, love and hope. Notice that each one is busy. Faith works. Love labours, and the word Paul uses for ‘labor’ means hard, tiring toil. Hope endures; it keeps going under a heavy load. For Paul these are not feelings to have but lives to live. And the hope has a name. It is ‘hope in our Lord Jesus Christ’, the hope of his coming, which will fill the end of every chapter of this letter.

Paul says he remembers them ‘always’ and ‘continually’. He had been torn away from these people only months before, and he could not stop thinking about them.
passages.ot:
‘Grace and peace’ gathers up the old blessing that Israel's priests spoke over the people: “the LORD lift up His countenance toward you and give you peace” (Numbers 6:26).

Waiting in hope for the Lord is a thread that runs through the Psalms and the Prophets. “I wait for the LORD; my soul does wait, and in His word I put my hope” (Psalm 130:5). “But those who wait upon the LORD will renew their strength” (Isaiah 40:31). The endurance Paul praises is that kind of waiting: not idle, but strong.

And love that labours is what the law asked of God's people from the start: “love your neighbor as yourself” (Leviticus 19:18).
passages.asks: Paul thanks God for three things he could see in this church: faith that works, love that labours, and hope that keeps going. Ask which of the three people could see in you, and which is weakest. Ask whom you thank God for, and whether you have told them. And ask where your hope is fixed, on things going well, or on the Lord Jesus Christ.

passages.t: Chosen, and an example to others
passages.happening:
Paul says, “Brothers who are beloved by God, we know that He has chosen you, because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with great conviction—just as you know we lived among you for your sake” (verses 4-5).

“And you became imitators of us and of the Lord when you welcomed the message with the joy of the Holy Spirit, in spite of your great suffering” (verse 6). So they became an example to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia (verse 7). “For not only did the message of the Lord ring out from you to Macedonia and Achaia, but your faith in God has gone out to every place, so that we have no need to say anything more” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
How can Paul say he knows God has chosen them? He does not claim to have seen a secret list. He points to what happened. The message came with power and the Holy Spirit. They welcomed it with joy, even when it cost them. Paul reads God's choice from its fruit. That is a comfort, not a puzzle. Their faith was not their own lucky guess. God was at work in it from the start.

The word for ‘conviction’ means full assurance, a deep certainty. And notice the last words of verse 5: the message was matched by the way the messengers lived. The Thessalonians had watched them, and the watching mattered as much as the words.

‘Great suffering’ was real. Acts tells of a mob, of Paul's host Jason dragged before the city officials, and of the missionaries sent away by night (Acts 17:5-10). After they left, the believers kept facing hostility from their neighbours (2:14). In a Greek city, a person who stopped honouring the gods could look disloyal to family and city. Yet they received the word ‘with the joy of the Holy Spirit’. Joy and suffering came together. That is not cheerfulness pasted over pain. It is a gladness that the pain could not take away.

They became ‘imitators of us and of the Lord’. In that world a student learned by copying a teacher's life, not only by memorising his words. And now the copied have become the example. Macedonia was the northern part of Greece and Achaia the southern part, with Corinth as its capital. Thessalonica was a port on the great Roman road, and news travelled along it with every merchant and traveller. The story of what happened in this church had run ahead of Paul. He says, a little proudly, that he hardly needs to tell it.
passages.ot:
God's choosing of his people has always rested on his love, not on their size or worth. Moses told Israel, “The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than the other peoples, for you were the fewest of all peoples. But because the LORD loved you” (Deuteronomy 7:7-8). Paul calls the Thessalonians ‘beloved by God’ in the same breath as ‘chosen’.

God's word does its work: “so My word that proceeds from My mouth will not return to Me empty, but it will accomplish what I please” (Isaiah 55:11).

And the word ringing out to every place fulfils the old hope that the nations would hear. God told his servant, “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6).
passages.hard:
Does ‘He has chosen you’ mean that God chooses some people and not others?

Christians have long thought hard about God's choosing, and they read it in different ways. Many in the Reformed tradition hold that God chose particular people for salvation before they could do anything, out of his free grace. Many in the Arminian and Wesleyan traditions hold that God's choice rests on his knowing who would believe, or that he chose Christ and all who are in him. Others stress that God chose a people, the church, rather than each person one by one. These notes do not choose. The site's note on Ephesians 1:3-14 sets out the views more fully, and the Honest Answer ‘Does God choose us, or do we choose Him?’ goes further.

What every view agrees on is what Paul does with the word here. He does not use it to make anyone anxious, or to shut anyone out. He uses it to give thanks, and to tell a frightened young church that their faith did not begin with them. God loved them first.

If you have ever been afraid that you are not one of the chosen, notice how Paul knew these people were. He saw that they had welcomed the message about Jesus and turned to God. The way to Christ is open: “Turn to Me and be saved, all the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 45:22).
passages.asks: Paul says the Thessalonians learned by watching how he lived, and then others learned by watching them. Ask who has been an example of faith to you, and what you copied. Ask who might be watching you, and what they are learning. And ask whether your faith has a joy in it that hard times have not been able to take away.

passages.t: From idols to the living God, waiting for his Son
passages.happening: People everywhere are talking about the Thessalonians. “For they themselves report what kind of welcome you gave us, and how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God and to await His Son from heaven, whom He raised from the dead—Jesus our deliverer from the coming wrath” (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
These two verses are so short and so full that many scholars think they echo the way the first missionaries summed up their message to people who worshipped idols. Turn. Serve. Wait. In one sentence they hold the whole story of a Christian.

First, they ‘turned to God from idols’. Notice the order. They turned to God, and so away from idols. In Thessalonica the gods were everywhere: in family meals, in the feasts of the trade guilds, in the city's festivals, and in the honours paid to Rome and its emperors. To stop honouring them meant pulling out of a great deal of ordinary life, and it could look like a danger to the city, since people believed the gods protected it. That is part of why the church suffered.

Second, they turned ‘to serve the living and true God’. An idol was a made thing, silent and still. The God they now served was alive, and real, and he had acted.

Third, they turned ‘to await His Son from heaven’. The word for ‘await’ is used only here in the New Testament. It means to wait for someone who is certain to come. Their faith leaned forward. They served God now, while they waited for Jesus.

Then comes a short creed. Jesus is God's Son. God raised him from the dead. He is in heaven, and he is coming. And he is ‘our deliverer from the coming wrath’. Wrath here is God's settled opposition to all that is evil, which the prophets said would come on the Day of the Lord. Jesus does not leave his people to face it alone. He rescues them.
passages.ot:
The prophets mocked idols and called the LORD ‘the living God’. “Their idols are silver and gold, made by the hands of men. They have mouths, but cannot speak” (Psalm 115:4-5). “But the LORD is the true God; He is the living God and eternal King” (Jeremiah 10:10).

Turning from idols to serve the LORD alone was Israel's call again and again. Samuel told the people, “rid yourselves of the foreign gods and Ashtoreths among you, prepare your hearts for the LORD, and serve Him only” (1 Samuel 7:3). And Jeremiah foresaw the nations doing what the Thessalonians did. He said to the LORD, “the nations will come to You from the ends of the earth”, confessing that their fathers had inherited ‘nothing but lies, worthless idols’ (Jeremiah 16:19).

Waiting for the God who saves is the hope of Isaiah: “Surely this is our God; we have waited for Him, and He has saved us” (Isaiah 25:9). And ‘the coming wrath’ is the prophets' Day of the LORD, “a day of wrath, a day of trouble and distress” (Zephaniah 1:15).
passages.hard:
Few people today bow down to a statue. What could ‘idols’ mean now?

In the Bible an idol is anything that takes the place of God: something we trust to keep us safe, look to for our worth, or serve with our time and love as though it were God. That can be money, success, comfort, a nation, a party, a person, or our own reputation. Good things become idols when we ask them to be God for us. The Thessalonians' idols stood in temples. Ours are often harder to see, but they are just as unable to save. The site's doctrine study ‘Idolatry’ says more.

And what of ‘the coming wrath’? God's wrath is not a bad temper. It is his steady and just opposition to evil, the evil that hurts his world and the people in it. A God who did not oppose evil would not be good. Paul's point is that Jesus rescues his people from it. The good news is not that there is no judgment. It is that there is a deliverer.
passages.asks: Turn, serve, wait: that was the shape of these new believers' lives. Ask what you have turned from, and what still competes with God for your trust. Ask whether your faith is something you serve with, or only something you hold. And ask whether you are waiting for Jesus, or living as though he will never come.
